materials.official_statement: Propositional and first order logic. Sets, relations, functions, partial orders and lattices. Monoids, Groups. Graphs: connectivity, matching, colouring. Combinatorics: counting, recurrence relations, generating functions.
materials.content_label: GATEPath original study note · mapped to official topic scope
materials.overview: Discrete mathematics studies finite structures and precise reasoning. Build fluency in translating statements into logic, testing relation properties, proving claims, and counting configurations.
learning_outcomes: Explain discrete mathematics using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: Propositional and first-order logic, Sets, relations and functions, Partial orders and lattices.
Identify assumptions, constraints and common sources of error.

concepts.heading: Logic and proof
concepts.explanation: Use truth tables, implication, equivalence, predicates and quantifiers. A proof should state assumptions, the claim and the reasoning rule used.

concepts.heading: Relations and order
concepts.explanation: A relation may be reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric or transitive. Equivalence relations partition a set; partial orders organise elements into comparable and incomparable pairs.

concepts.heading: Graphs and counting
concepts.explanation: Represent a graph as vertices and edges. Connectivity, paths, matchings and colourings describe structure; counting arguments use product, sum, permutations, combinations and recurrences.

worked_example.prompt: A set has 5 distinct elements. The number of ways to choose 2 without order is C(5,2) = 5!/(2!3!) = 10. If order mattered, the answer would be 5×4 = 20.
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: Combination
formula_cards.note: Choose r items from n when order does not matter.

formula_cards.name: Product rule
formula_cards.note: For independent sequential choices, multiply the number of options.

common_mistakes: Confusing implication with equivalence.
Assuming a relation is an equivalence relation after checking only two properties.
Using permutations when the selected items are unordered.
quick_revision: Write the definition before testing a relation.
For a graph question, identify vertices, edges, direction and connectivity first.
For counting, decide whether order and repetition matter.

materials.official_statement: Matrices, determinants, system of linear equations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, LU decomposition.
materials.content_label: GATEPath original study note · mapped to official topic scope
materials.overview: Linear algebra describes systems of linear equations and transformations using matrices and vectors. GATE problems commonly connect rank, consistency, determinants, eigenvalues and matrix factorisation.
learning_outcomes: Explain linear algebra using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: Matrices and determinants, Systems of linear equations, Eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
Identify assumptions, constraints and common sources of error.

concepts.heading: Systems and rank
concepts.explanation: For Ax=b, compare rank(A) and rank([A|b]). A consistent system has equal ranks; uniqueness additionally requires the rank to equal the number of unknowns.

concepts.heading: Determinants and inverse
concepts.explanation: A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is non-zero. Elementary row operations affect determinants in defined ways.

concepts.heading: Eigenvalues and LU
concepts.explanation: Eigenpairs satisfy Av=λv for non-zero v. LU decomposition factors A into lower and upper triangular matrices, enabling efficient repeated solves.

worked_example.prompt: For A = [[2,0],[0,3]], the characteristic equation is (2−λ)(3−λ)=0, so the eigenvalues are 2 and 3.
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: Characteristic equation
formula_cards.note: Roots give the eigenvalues of a square matrix.

formula_cards.name: Trace and determinant
formula_cards.expression: sum of eigenvalues = trace(A); product of eigenvalues = det(A)
formula_cards.note: Count algebraic multiplicity over the complex numbers.

common_mistakes: Treating a non-square matrix as invertible.
Forgetting that eigenvectors must be non-zero.
Applying a row-swap or row-scaling without updating a determinant calculation.
quick_revision: Check matrix dimensions before multiplying.
Use rank to test consistency.
Verify an eigenpair by substituting into Av=λv.

materials.official_statement: Limits, continuity and differentiability, Maxima and minima, Mean value theorem, Integration.
materials.content_label: GATEPath original study note · mapped to official topic scope
materials.overview: Calculus studies limits, derivatives and integrals. For GATE, focus on continuity, differentiability, extrema, mean value results and interpreting definite integrals.
learning_outcomes: Explain calculus using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: Limits, continuity and differentiability, Maxima and minima, Mean value theorem.
Identify assumptions, constraints and common sources of error.

concepts.heading: Limits and continuity
concepts.explanation: A limit describes the value approached near a point. Continuity at a requires the function value and two-sided limit to exist and agree.

concepts.heading: Differentiation and extrema
concepts.explanation: The derivative is the instantaneous rate of change. Interior differentiable extrema require f′(x)=0, but candidate points must be checked.

concepts.heading: Integration
concepts.explanation: A definite integral is accumulated signed area. The fundamental theorem links differentiation and integration.

worked_example.prompt: For f(x)=x²−4x+1, f′(x)=2x−4. The stationary point is x=2; f′′(2)=2>0, so it is a local minimum.
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: Power rule
formula_cards.note: For differentiable powers in the usual domain.

formula_cards.name: Fundamental theorem
formula_cards.note: Evaluate a definite integral using an antiderivative.

common_mistakes: Assuming f′(x)=0 always means a maximum or minimum.
Ignoring endpoints when finding absolute extrema on a closed interval.
Confusing signed area with geometric area.
quick_revision: Check domain and one-sided limits.
Classify stationary points using derivative tests.
Include endpoints in closed-interval optimisation.

materials.official_statement: Random variables, Uniform, normal, exponential, Poisson and binomial distributions. Mean, median, mode and standard deviation. Conditional probability and Bayes theorem.
materials.content_label: GATEPath original study note · mapped to official topic scope
materials.overview: Probability quantifies uncertainty; statistics summarises data. Distinguish a random variable from an event, and choose a distribution from the experiment’s assumptions.
learning_outcomes: Explain probability and statistics using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: Random variables, Uniform, normal, exponential, Poisson and binomial distributions, Mean, median, mode and standard deviation.
Identify assumptions, constraints and common sources of error.

concepts.heading: Events and conditional probability
concepts.explanation: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), for P(B)>0. Independence means P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).

concepts.heading: Distributions
concepts.explanation: Binomial counts successes in a fixed number of independent equal-probability trials; Poisson models counts over exposure; normal is continuous and symmetric; exponential models waiting times.

concepts.heading: Summary measures
concepts.explanation: Expectation is a probability-weighted average. Variance measures squared spread; standard deviation is its square root. Median and mode describe different aspects of a distribution.

worked_example.prompt: If P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5 and P(A∩B)=0.2, then P(A|B)=0.2/0.5=0.4. Here A and B are independent.
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: Bayes theorem
formula_cards.note: Update a prior probability using observed evidence.

formula_cards.name: Variance
formula_cards.note: Population variance for a random variable.

formula_cards.name: Binomial mean/variance
formula_cards.note: For X~Binomial(n,p).

common_mistakes: Adding probabilities of overlapping events without subtracting the intersection.
Using binomial assumptions when trials are dependent.
Mixing variance and standard deviation.
quick_revision: List the sample space or events first.
Check independence and distribution assumptions.
Keep units and parameters clear.

materials.official_statement: Boolean algebra and minimization – algebraic technique, Karnaugh map, tabular method.
materials.content_label: GATEPath original study note · mapped to official topic scope
materials.overview: Boolean algebra manipulates binary-valued expressions. Minimisation seeks an equivalent expression with fewer literals or gates while preserving the truth table.
learning_outcomes: Explain boolean algebra and minimization using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: Boolean algebra, Algebraic minimization technique, Karnaugh map.
Identify assumptions, constraints and common sources of error.

concepts.heading: Core laws
concepts.explanation: Use identity, null, idempotent, complement, absorption, distributive and De Morgan laws to transform expressions.

concepts.heading: Canonical forms
concepts.explanation: A sum of minterms is an SOP representation; a product of maxterms is a POS representation. Each truth-table row maps systematically to a term.

concepts.heading: K-map and tabulation
concepts.explanation: Karnaugh maps group adjacent 1s (or 0s) in powers of two, including wrap-around adjacency. The tabular method performs systematic combining and is useful when variables increase.

worked_example.prompt: A + A′B = (A + A′)(A + B) = A + B. This is the absorption/consensus-style simplification often used before gate implementation.
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: De Morgan
formula_cards.note: Complement an entire product or sum.

formula_cards.name: XOR
formula_cards.note: Output is 1 when inputs differ.

common_mistakes: Grouping K-map cells diagonally; only edge-adjacent groups are valid.
Using non-power-of-two group sizes.
Forgetting wrap-around adjacency.
quick_revision: Derive minterms carefully from variable order.
Use the largest valid groups.
Verify the simplified expression against the truth table.

materials.official_statement: Design of combinational and sequential circuits.
materials.content_label: GATEPath original study note · mapped to official topic scope
materials.overview: Combinational circuits produce outputs from current inputs; sequential circuits also depend on stored state. Design requires truth tables, Boolean equations and state reasoning.
learning_outcomes: Explain combinational and sequential circuits using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: Design of combinational circuits, Design of sequential circuits.
Identify assumptions, constraints and common sources of error.

concepts.heading: Combinational blocks
concepts.explanation: Adders, subtractors, multiplexers, decoders, encoders and comparators have no memory. Derive each output as a Boolean function of inputs.

concepts.heading: Sequential blocks
concepts.explanation: Latches and flip-flops store state. A clocked circuit updates state on a triggering edge or level according to its device model.

concepts.heading: State machines
concepts.explanation: A finite-state machine uses state transition and output logic. Mealy outputs depend on state and inputs; Moore outputs depend on state.

worked_example.prompt: A 2:1 multiplexer has Y = S′I₀ + SI₁. When S=0 it selects I₀; when S=1 it selects I₁.
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: Full-adder sum
formula_cards.note: Sum output of a one-bit full adder.

formula_cards.name: Full-adder carry
formula_cards.note: Carry is 1 when at least two inputs are 1.

common_mistakes: Treating a sequential circuit as purely combinational.
Mixing present-state and next-state variables.
Ignoring setup/hold timing when reasoning about a clocked system.
quick_revision: Draw the truth table first.
Name state variables explicitly.
Check reset and clock assumptions.

materials.official_statement: Number representation and arithmetic (fixed and floating point).
materials.content_label: GATEPath original study note · mapped to official topic scope
materials.overview: Computer arithmetic represents signed and real values in finite bit patterns. Understand ranges, overflow, rounding and the difference between representation and mathematical values.
learning_outcomes: Explain number representation and arithmetic using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: Fixed-point number representation and arithmetic, Floating-point number representation and arithmetic.
Identify assumptions, constraints and common sources of error.

concepts.heading: Integer representation
concepts.explanation: Unsigned n-bit values range from 0 to 2ⁿ−1. Two’s-complement signed values range from −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹−1.

concepts.heading: Two’s complement
concepts.explanation: Negation is formed by inverting bits and adding one. Sign extension replicates the sign bit when widening.

concepts.heading: Floating point
concepts.explanation: A floating-point number is represented using sign, exponent and significand fields. Finite precision causes rounding and spacing between representable values.

worked_example.prompt: In 8-bit two’s complement, +5 is 00000101. Invert and add one: 11111010 + 1 = 11111011, which represents −5.
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: Unsigned range
formula_cards.note: Range for n bits.

formula_cards.name: Two’s-complement range
formula_cards.note: Range for n-bit signed values.

formula_cards.name: Normalized binary value
formula_cards.note: Conceptual form for a normalized binary float.

common_mistakes: Assuming overflow wraps identically for all arithmetic formats.
Negating the most negative two’s-complement number in the same width.
Comparing floating-point values as exact real numbers.
quick_revision: Identify signed or unsigned before calculating.
Check representable range after every operation.
Distinguish precision, range and rounding.

materials.overview: An instruction set architecture defines the visible contract between software and a processor: operations, registers, data types, memory access and addressing modes.
learning_outcomes: Explain instruction set and addressing modes using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: Instruction set, Addressing modes.

concepts.heading: Instruction fields
concepts.explanation: An instruction may encode an opcode, register identifiers, immediate values and addressing information.

concepts.heading: Addressing modes
concepts.explanation: Immediate embeds a constant; register uses a register; direct/absolute identifies a memory address; indirect uses an address stored elsewhere; indexed combines a base and offset.

concepts.heading: Effective address
concepts.explanation: Translate the mode into the effective address before counting memory accesses or tracing execution.

worked_example.prompt: If a base register contains 1000 and the instruction uses displacement 24, base-plus-offset addressing accesses address 1024 (assuming byte addressing).
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: Byte address
formula_cards.note: Common base/offset addressing calculation.

formula_cards.name: Instruction size
formula_cards.note: Field widths must fit the instruction format.

common_mistakes: Confusing the address of a pointer with the value stored at that address.
Forgetting whether addresses are byte- or word-addressed.
Counting an immediate operand as an extra data-memory access.
quick_revision: Parse the addressing mode first.
Write register and memory values in a trace table.
Count instruction fetches separately from data accesses.

materials.official_statement: Design of arithmetic and logic unit (ALU).
materials.content_label: GATEPath original study note · mapped to official topic scope
materials.overview: An arithmetic logic unit performs arithmetic and bitwise operations selected by control inputs. Design problems combine truth tables, adders, multiplexers and status flags.
learning_outcomes: Explain arithmetic and logic unit using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: ALU design.
Identify assumptions, constraints and common sources of error.

concepts.heading: Datapath view
concepts.explanation: Operands enter functional blocks; control signals select operations; the result and condition flags leave the ALU.

concepts.heading: Arithmetic
concepts.explanation: Addition and subtraction share an adder by complementing one operand and setting carry-in for two’s-complement subtraction.

concepts.heading: Flags
concepts.explanation: Zero, carry, sign and overflow flags summarise result properties; carry and signed overflow are not the same condition.

worked_example.prompt: A − B can be implemented as A + (two’s-complement of B). For n bits, use A + B′ + 1.
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: Subtraction
formula_cards.note: n-bit two’s-complement arithmetic.

formula_cards.name: Signed overflow
formula_cards.expression: For addition: operands have same sign and result has opposite sign
formula_cards.note: A bit-level condition for signed two’s-complement overflow.

common_mistakes: Equating carry-out with signed overflow.
Forgetting to invert B and add carry-in for subtraction.
Ignoring result width.
quick_revision: Track width at every stage.
Interpret flags according to signed or unsigned operation.
Check boundary cases such as largest positive plus one.

materials.official_statement: Design of control unit – hardwired and microprogrammed.
materials.content_label: GATEPath original study note · mapped to official topic scope
materials.overview: The control unit sequences processor micro-operations. Hardwired control uses logic circuits; microprogrammed control uses control words stored in a control memory.
learning_outcomes: Explain control unit using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: Hardwired control unit, Microprogrammed control unit.
Identify assumptions, constraints and common sources of error.

concepts.heading: Hardwired control
concepts.explanation: Control outputs are generated by combinational/sequential logic from instruction bits, timing and status signals.

concepts.heading: Microprogrammed control
concepts.explanation: A microinstruction specifies control signals and next-address behaviour. A microprogram is a sequence of microinstructions.

concepts.heading: Trade-offs
concepts.explanation: Hardwired control can be fast but is less flexible to modify. Microprogramming can simplify complex control sequencing but adds control-store access.

worked_example.prompt: A fetch sequence may contain MAR←PC, MDR←Memory[MAR], IR←MDR and PC←PC+1. Exact timing depends on the processor design.
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: Control word
formula_cards.expression: A bit field representing one or more control signals
formula_cards.note: Interpret the encoding provided in the problem.

formula_cards.name: Microsequence
formula_cards.expression: µPC(next) = branch target or sequential address
formula_cards.note: Next microinstruction depends on sequencing logic.

common_mistakes: Assuming one universal fetch microsequence for every architecture.
Confusing datapath registers with control-store registers.
Assuming every control signal is active-high.
quick_revision: Separate control sequencing from datapath operation.
Follow the problem’s timing and signal conventions.
Draw the micro-operation sequence.

materials.official_statement: Memory interfacing and hierarchy: performance, cache memory mapping.
materials.content_label: GATEPath original study note · mapped to official topic scope
materials.overview: Memory hierarchy balances speed, capacity and cost using registers, caches, main memory and secondary storage. Cache questions often test address decomposition and average access time.
learning_outcomes: Explain memory interfacing and hierarchy using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: Memory interfacing, Memory hierarchy and performance, Cache memory mapping.
Identify assumptions, constraints and common sources of error.

concepts.heading: Locality
concepts.explanation: Temporal locality means recently used data may be reused; spatial locality means nearby addresses may be accessed.

concepts.heading: Mapping
concepts.explanation: Direct-mapped caches assign each memory block to one line; fully associative caches allow any line; set-associative caches allow a block in one set.

concepts.heading: Performance
concepts.explanation: Hit ratio, miss penalty and access time determine effective memory performance. Write policies and replacement policies affect traffic and behaviour.

worked_example.prompt: A 32-bit byte address with 64-byte blocks uses 6 offset bits. If the cache has 256 sets, the index needs 8 bits; remaining 18 bits are tag bits.
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: AMAT
formula_cards.expression: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty
formula_cards.note: Single-level cache average memory access time.

formula_cards.name: Address split
formula_cards.expression: address bits = tag + index + block offset
formula_cards.note: For a power-of-two cache/block configuration.

common_mistakes: Using cache capacity instead of number of sets to calculate index bits.
Forgetting byte offset bits.
Treating a write-through policy as write-back.
quick_revision: Convert sizes into powers of two.
Draw tag/index/offset fields before solving.
Check hit and miss cases separately.

materials.overview: I/O systems connect processors and peripherals. Interrupts allow devices to request service; DMA transfers blocks between devices and memory with limited CPU intervention.
learning_outcomes: Explain i/o interface using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: Interrupts, Direct memory access (DMA).
Identify assumptions, constraints and common sources of error.

concepts.heading: Programmed I/O
concepts.explanation: The CPU repeatedly checks device status and moves data, which may waste processor time.

concepts.heading: Interrupt-driven I/O
concepts.explanation: A device signals the CPU when service is needed. The CPU saves context, runs an interrupt handler and resumes execution.

concepts.heading: DMA
concepts.explanation: A DMA controller manages a block transfer after the CPU configures source, destination, size and direction. Completion may raise an interrupt.

worked_example.prompt: For a 4 KiB disk block, programmed I/O may require CPU-mediated word transfers, while DMA can move the block after setup and notify the CPU on completion.
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: Transfer time
formula_cards.expression: T ≈ setup time + data size / transfer rate
formula_cards.note: A simplified model; include bus contention when specified.

formula_cards.name: Interrupt rate
formula_cards.expression: interrupts per second = event rate / items per interrupt
formula_cards.note: Useful when one interrupt services a batch.

common_mistakes: Assuming DMA means the CPU is never involved.
Confusing an interrupt with a polling loop.
Ignoring transfer setup and completion overhead.
quick_revision: Compare CPU involvement, latency and throughput.
Identify who owns the bus during DMA.
Trace the interrupt service lifecycle.

materials.overview: Pipelining overlaps instruction stages to improve throughput. Hazards prevent an instruction from proceeding safely and may require stalls, forwarding or prediction.
learning_outcomes: Explain instruction pipelining using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: Instruction pipelining, Pipeline hazards.
Identify assumptions, constraints and common sources of error.

concepts.heading: Pipeline timing
concepts.explanation: A k-stage pipeline ideally completes one instruction per cycle after filling, but stage imbalance and hazards reduce throughput.

concepts.heading: Data and control hazards
concepts.explanation: A data hazard occurs when an instruction depends on an earlier result. A control hazard comes from branches or changes in instruction flow.

concepts.heading: Structural hazards
concepts.explanation: Two operations require the same hardware resource in the same cycle. Replication or scheduling may remove the conflict.

worked_example.prompt: A 5-stage pipeline processing 8 instructions ideally takes 5 + 8 − 1 = 12 cycles, assuming one cycle per stage and no stalls.
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: Ideal cycles
formula_cards.note: For n instructions in a k-stage pipeline, with no stalls.

formula_cards.name: Speedup
formula_cards.note: Use actual stage times and stall cycles when provided.

common_mistakes: Using ideal pipeline timing when stalls are present.

formula_cards.note: As n grows, each later class eventually dominates earlier ones.

concepts.heading: Decidable and recognisable
concepts.explanation: A decidable language has a machine that halts on every input. A recogniser accepts members but may loop on non-members.

concepts.heading: Undecidability
concepts.explanation: Diagonalisation and reductions establish limits. To prove A undecidable, reduce a known undecidable problem to A with a computable transformation.

formula_cards.note: A safe state guarantees at least one completion order.

Mixing safe state with deadlock-free current execution only.
Forgetting to release allocations when simulating completion.

concepts.heading: Keys and nulls

formula_cards.name: Selection

formula_cards.name: Projection

formula_cards.name: Natural join
formula_cards.note: Matches equal common attributes; check attribute names and domains.

Ignoring NULL in comparisons and NOT IN subqueries.

materials.overview: Integrity constraints protect valid database states. Normalisation reduces undesirable dependency-driven redundancy while preserving required information.
learning_outcomes: Explain integrity constraints and normal forms using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: Integrity constraints, Normal forms.
Identify assumptions, constraints and common sources of error.

concepts.heading: Constraints
concepts.explanation: Domain, key, entity integrity and referential integrity constrain valid values and references.

concepts.heading: Functional dependencies
concepts.explanation: X→Y means equal X values imply equal Y values. Attribute closure helps test superkeys and candidate keys.

concepts.heading: Normal forms
concepts.explanation: 1NF requires atomic values in the chosen model; 2NF removes partial dependency of non-prime attributes on candidate-key subsets; 3NF and BCNF impose stronger dependency conditions.

worked_example.prompt: In Student(course_id, course_name, instructor), if course_id→course_name,instructor and each row repeats course data for many students, decompose course data into a Course relation and reference it.
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: Closure
formula_cards.expression: X⁺ = attributes functionally implied by X
formula_cards.note: Compute iteratively using the given FDs.

formula_cards.name: 3NF condition
formula_cards.expression: For every nontrivial X→A: X is a superkey or A is prime
formula_cards.note: A is prime if it belongs to some candidate key.

formula_cards.name: BCNF
formula_cards.expression: For every nontrivial X→Y, X is a superkey
formula_cards.note: Stronger than 3NF.

common_mistakes: Finding only one candidate key and stopping.
Using 2NF reasoning without considering all candidate keys.
Assuming BCNF decomposition always preserves dependencies.
quick_revision: Compute closures to find keys.
Identify prime attributes.
Check losslessness and dependency preservation separately.

concepts.heading: Index costs

formula_cards.name: B+ tree range scan
formula_cards.note: Linked leaves make range access efficient.

Ignoring page I/O versus CPU comparisons.
Assuming a secondary index is always clustered.
quick_revision: Identify order/fan-out convention.
Count levels and page reads exactly as defined.
Separate point lookup and range scan costs.

materials.overview: Transactions group database actions into a logical unit. Concurrency control preserves isolation and serialisable behaviour while recovery handles failures.

Solve standard problems related to: Transactions, Concurrency control.
Identify assumptions, constraints and common sources of error.

concepts.heading: ACID
concepts.explanation: Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability describe transaction properties.

concepts.heading: Schedules and serializability
concepts.explanation: A schedule interleaves operations. Conflict serializability can be tested with a precedence graph; acyclic graphs imply conflict-serialisable schedules.

concepts.heading: Concurrency and recovery
concepts.explanation: Locks, timestamps and validation are control techniques. Logs support undo/redo; checkpoints reduce recovery work.

worked_example.prompt: If T1 writes X before T2 reads X, add T1→T2 in the conflict graph when those operations conflict. A cycle means the schedule is not conflict-serialisable.
worked_example.note: This is an original learning illustration, not a past GATE examination question.

formula_cards.name: Conflict
formula_cards.expression: same data item + different transactions + at least one write
formula_cards.note: Identifies ordering constraints.

formula_cards.name: 2PL
formula_cards.expression: growing phase acquires; shrinking phase releases
formula_cards.note: Basic two-phase locking ensures conflict serializability.

formula_cards.name: Strict 2PL
formula_cards.note: Prevents cascading aborts under the standard model.

common_mistakes: Adding graph edges for read-read pairs.
Confusing conflict serializability with view serializability.
Assuming every lock protocol prevents deadlock.
quick_revision: List conflicting pairs in schedule order.
Build the precedence graph.
For recovery, identify log records and commit/checkpoint boundaries.

concepts.heading: Service and protocol

Treating a service interface as a peer protocol.

materials.overview: Switching determines how information traverses a network. Performance metrics quantify delay, throughput, loss and resource use.
learning_outcomes: Explain switching and performance metrics using precise definitions and examples.
Solve standard problems related to: Circuit switching, Packet switching, Virtual circuit switching.

concepts.heading: Switching
concepts.explanation: Circuit switching reserves a path/resource; packet switching shares links by packets; virtual-circuit switching uses connection-like forwarding state.

concepts.heading: Transmission vs propagation
concepts.explanation: Transmission delay depends on packet bits and link rate; propagation delay depends on distance and signal speed.

concepts.heading: Queueing and throughput
concepts.explanation: Congestion creates queueing delay and possible loss. End-to-end throughput is constrained by bottlenecks along the path.

worked_example.prompt: A 1500-byte packet on a 10 Mb/s link has transmission delay 1500×8 / 10,000,000 = 1.2 ms, excluding other delays.

formula_cards.name: Transmission delay
formula_cards.note: L bits, R bits per second.

formula_cards.name: Propagation delay
formula_cards.note: Distance d divided by propagation speed v.

formula_cards.name: Bandwidth-delay product
formula_cards.note: Approximate bits that can be in flight across a path.

common_mistakes: Using bytes instead of bits in L/R.
Adding propagation delay as if it depended on packet length.
Confusing link bandwidth with achieved throughput.
quick_revision: Convert all quantities to consistent units.
Calculate each delay component separately.
Identify the bottleneck link.

concepts.explanation: Frames delimit packets. Checksums/CRC detect certain error patterns but do not necessarily correct errors.

concepts.heading: MAC
concepts.explanation: Protocols coordinate access to shared media. Ethernet historically used CSMA/CD in half-duplex shared media; modern switched full-duplex Ethernet does not use collision detection in the same way.

concepts.heading: Ethernet and switching

formula_cards.name: Stop-and-wait utilisation
formula_cards.note: a = propagation time / frame transmission time; assumptions matter.

Applying CSMA/CD assumptions to full-duplex switched Ethernet.
Confusing MAC and IP addresses.

Write CRC steps using XOR.
Separate framing, error detection and medium access.

concepts.heading: Connection and reliability
concepts.explanation: Sequence numbers identify byte positions; acknowledgements report received sequence space. Retransmission repairs loss.

concepts.heading: Flow control
concepts.explanation: The receiver advertises a receive window so the sender does not overrun receiver buffers.

concepts.heading: Congestion control
concepts.explanation: TCP adjusts the sending rate using congestion signals and a congestion window. Slow start, congestion avoidance and loss response are classic mechanisms.

formula_cards.name: Sequence number

formula_cards.name: Bandwidth-delay product
formula_cards.note: A useful scale for the amount of data in flight.

Treating TCP as message-oriented rather than a byte stream.
Off-by-one mistakes in ACK/sequence calculations.

concepts.heading: Vocabulary in context
concepts.explanation: Use the sentence around a word as evidence. Look for contrast markers (although, however), cause markers (because, therefore), examples and the overall tone. Distinguish close options by connotation and grammatical role, not by vague familiarity.

concepts.heading: Reading comprehension
concepts.explanation: Read the question stem carefully, locate the relevant paragraph and support every answer with a line or a necessary inference. Main-idea questions require the central claim; detail questions require specific evidence; inference questions must not introduce assumptions absent from the passage.

concepts.heading: Narrative sequencing
concepts.explanation: Find the opening sentence, identify pronouns and demonstratives that refer backward, track chronology and causal links, and use transition words to connect the paragraph. A sentence beginning with “this”, “such” or “therefore” usually needs an earlier referent.

worked_example.title: Sentence order using reference clues
worked_example.prompt: Arrange: (P) This method reduces repeated work. (Q) A search tree stores keys in an ordered structure. (R) Therefore, lookup can discard part of the remaining search space. (S) Its ordering property is the key to the reduction.
steps: Q introduces the subject: a search tree.
S refers to the ordering property of the structure just introduced.
P explains the consequence of the method.
R begins with “therefore” and concludes the causal chain.

common_mistakes: Choosing an option because it sounds sophisticated rather than because the passage supports it.
Treating an inference as permission to add outside facts.
Ignoring pronoun references and transition words in sentence ordering.
Checking a verb against the nearest noun instead of the grammatical subject.
quick_revision: Subject first, then verb agreement.
Use surrounding clauses to infer vocabulary.
Every comprehension answer needs textual evidence.
For ordering, track references, chronology and connectors.

materials.official_statement: Data interpretation using bar graphs, pie charts, other graphs, 2D/3D plots, maps and tables; ratios, percentages, powers, exponents and logarithms; permutations and combinations; series; mensuration and geometry; elementary statistics and probability.
materials.content_label: GATEPath original study note · scope mapped to official GATE 2027 GA syllabus
materials.overview: Quantitative Aptitude combines arithmetic fluency with interpretation of data and elementary mathematical reasoning. Work with units, estimates and exact definitions. In chart questions, read the axes, legend, scale and time period before calculating.
learning_outcomes: Interpret values from tables, maps, bar and pie charts and 2D/3D plots.
Solve ratio, percentage and proportional reasoning problems.
Use indices, exponents and logarithms correctly.
Count arrangements and selections using permutations and combinations.
Solve elementary series, geometry, mensuration, statistics and probability questions.

concepts.heading: Data interpretation workflow
concepts.explanation: Read the title, axes, units, legend and scale. Record the requested population and time period. For a pie chart, value = sector fraction × total; for a rate or percentage, identify the correct denominator. Estimate first to catch arithmetic errors.

concepts.heading: Ratios and percentages
concepts.explanation: A:B = a:b means the quantities are ka and kb. Percentage change = (new − old) / old × 100. If a value rises by x% and later falls by x%, the original value is generally not restored. Convert percentages to fractions before long calculations when convenient.

concepts.heading: Powers, exponents and logarithms
concepts.explanation: Use a^m a^n = a^(m+n), (a^m)^n = a^(mn), and log_b(xy)=log_b x + log_b y for valid positive arguments and base b>0, b≠1. Check the domain before applying a logarithm or cancelling exponents.

concepts.heading: Counting and series
concepts.explanation: Use multiplication for sequential independent choices. Use nPr when order matters and nCr when only the selected set matters. For series, test first differences, second differences, ratios and alternating subsequences before assuming a familiar pattern.

concepts.heading: Geometry, mensuration and elementary statistics
concepts.explanation: Write the relevant area, perimeter or volume relation before substituting. Keep units consistent. Mean is sum/count; median is the middle after sorting; mode is most frequent; standard deviation measures spread around the mean.

concepts.heading: Probability
concepts.explanation: For equally likely outcomes, P(A)=favourable outcomes/total outcomes. For conditional probability, P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) when P(B)>0. Use Bayes’ theorem only after identifying the prior, likelihood and evidence probability.

worked_example.title: Percentage change
worked_example.prompt: A dataset contains 240 records. The count increases by 15%. What is the new count?

common_mistakes: Using the new value as the denominator for percentage change.
Ignoring units and chart scales.
Using permutations when order is irrelevant.
Applying logarithm laws to non-positive arguments.
Assuming events are independent without justification.
quick_revision: Read chart axes, units and legend first.
Percentage-change denominator is the original value.
Decide whether order matters before choosing nPr or nCr.
Check domains and units before finalising.

materials.official_statement: Logical deduction and induction; analogies; numerical relations and reasoning.
materials.content_label: GATEPath original study note · scope mapped to official GATE 2027 GA syllabus
materials.overview: Analytical Aptitude rewards structured reasoning. Translate statements into constraints, separate facts from assumptions and test candidate conclusions. For numerical relations and analogies, identify the rule that consistently maps each example.
learning_outcomes: Use deduction to identify conclusions that must follow from stated premises.
Use induction to recognise a pattern while distinguishing a conjecture from proof.
Solve analogies by identifying the relationship, not just surface similarity.
Translate numerical relations into equations or constraints.

concepts.heading: Deductive reasoning
concepts.explanation: A conclusion is valid only if it follows from the premises. For “all A are B” and “some B are C”, do not infer that some A are C. Use set diagrams, truth tables or short symbolic statements to test the exact implication.

concepts.heading: Inductive reasoning
concepts.explanation: Induction generalises from observed examples. Test more than one case and look for counterexamples. A pattern observed in a few terms may suggest a rule but is not a proof unless the question asks only for the next term under the intended pattern.

concepts.heading: Analogies
concepts.explanation: Name the relationship in the first pair (part-to-whole, tool-to-purpose, cause-to-effect, sequence, category or inverse) before evaluating options. Apply the same relationship in the same direction to the second pair.

concepts.heading: Numerical relations
concepts.explanation: Translate words into variables and constraints. Track signs, parity, divisibility, relative order and arithmetic operations. Check each option against every condition, not just the first.

worked_example.title: Set-based deduction
worked_example.prompt: All processors are hardware components. Some hardware components are programmable. Which statement must be true: (A) all processors are programmable, (B) some processors are programmable, (C) all processors are hardware components, (D) no hardware components are processors?
steps: Represent processors as a subset of hardware components.
The statement about some programmable hardware does not locate those items inside the processor subset.
Therefore neither A nor B is forced, while C repeats the first premise.

common_mistakes: Confusing “all” with “some”.
Assuming two sets overlap because each is related to a third set.
Treating an observed sequence as a unique mathematical rule.
Using only surface resemblance to solve an analogy.
quick_revision: A deduction must follow in every model satisfying the premises.
Induction suggests patterns; it does not prove them automatically.
State the analogy relationship before choosing an option.
Check every constraint in numerical reasoning.

materials.official_statement: Transformations such as translation, rotation, scaling, mirroring, assembling and grouping; paper folding and cutting; patterns in two and three dimensions.
materials.content_label: GATEPath original study note · scope mapped to official GATE 2027 GA syllabus
materials.overview: Spatial Aptitude tests mental manipulation of two- and three-dimensional objects. Track orientation, adjacency, visible faces and the effect of each transformation. Avoid assuming that a rotation changes shape or that a mirror image preserves left and right.
learning_outcomes: Track translation, rotation, scaling and mirroring.
Reason about assembling and grouping objects.
Predict outcomes of paper-folding and cutting operations.
Recognise patterns in 2D and 3D shapes.

concepts.heading: Transformations
concepts.explanation: Translation changes position but not orientation. Rotation changes orientation around a specified centre. Scaling changes dimensions while preserving shape under uniform scaling. Mirroring reflects across an axis or plane and reverses handedness.

concepts.heading: Assembling and grouping
concepts.explanation: Check edge lengths, orientation, matching faces, symmetry and whether pieces can touch without overlap. For 3D objects, keep track of which faces become adjacent after folding or assembly.

concepts.heading: Paper folding and cutting
concepts.explanation: Mentally unfold the paper in reverse order. A cut made through multiple folded layers is reflected across each fold line. Mark the fold axes and reflect each cut location systematically.

concepts.heading: 2D and 3D patterns
concepts.explanation: Look for rotation, reflection, translation, repetition, alternation, face-count changes, shading and adjacency. For cubes, distinguish the visible faces and test whether an option can result from rotation rather than reflection.

worked_example.title: Translation versus rotation
worked_example.prompt: A square is moved three units to the right without being turned or resized. Which geometric transformation describes this operation?
steps: Its orientation, side lengths and angles remain unchanged.
This is a translation, not rotation or scaling.

common_mistakes: Treating a mirror image as an ordinary rotation.
Forgetting the order of multiple folds.
Assuming scaling always preserves proportions when scaling may be non-uniform.
Ignoring which faces are adjacent in a folded 3D object.
quick_revision: Translation: position; rotation: orientation; scaling: size; reflection: reversed handedness.
Unfold paper cuts in reverse fold order.
Track axes, face adjacency and symmetry explicitly.
Use a small sketch or cube net to validate 3D reasoning.
